newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Lebed seeks comeback from Kremlin sacking.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed seeks comeback from Kremlin sacking.

text.p: Russia's popular strongman Alexander Lebed began the fight for his political comeback on Friday after being sacked by President Boris Yeltsin for making waves in the Kremlin.

Lebed's dismissal as secretary of Yeltsin's Security Council ends a four-month marriage of convenience between the general and the ailing president, who said he had got fed up with Lebed's argumentative character and presidential ambitions.
The Kremlin newspaper Rossiskiye Vesti greeted the sacking, announced by Yeltsin on television on Thursday, with a gleeful pun on Lebed's name, which means swan.
"The swan has flown away," it said in a banner headline.

But other commentators were not so convinced that Lebed's departure would end either the general's career or Russia's problems, which include mass delays in wage payments, a shaky peace in Chechnya and a president laid low with heart problems.
"The swan flew away yesterday. Where will Russia fly tomorrow?" said Komsomolskaya Pravda.
Lebed, who has denied charges by Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov that he was preparing a "creeping coup", warned that Russia was in for a "hot autumn".

He cited discontent in the crumbling army and the future of the Chechnya peace process he sponsored as Yeltsin's envoy to the rebel region. Interfax news agency quoted presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky as saying Lebed's dimissal from this post was only a matter of time.

"Whatever your attitude to Alexander Lebed...his sacking will lower tension in Moscow. The question is what might happen in Chechnya as a result?" said the liberal opposition daily Nezavisimaya Gazeta.

Rebel leaders in Chechnya, who view the August peace deal as a victory in their 21-month battle with Russia, announced plans on Friday to hold elections in the region on January 27 -- a move sure to upset Moscow, which says it should be consulted.

Lebed, who said after his sacking that he would have a good sleep and then start polishing his political machine for a presidential bid, was planning a visit to the theatre on Friday to see the play "Ivan the Terrible".
"I will learn how to rule the state," Interfax news agency quoted Lebed as saying with characteristic cynicism. The 16th century ruler was renowned for his cruelty and ruthlessness.
"That is, provided they do not deprive me of theatre tickets after my sacking," Lebed added.
Many members of the lower house of parliament, which met on Friday to discuss the political fallout from Lebed's dismissal, joined the establishment's vigorous criticism of the general.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov made clear he had little love for the man who could dent his support in a future poll.
"His 'romance' with Boris Yeltsin lasted only two or three months and it was a clear political bargain," Zyuganov said.
Lebed won his place on Yeltsin's team after coming third in the first round of the presidential election.

But since moving into the Kremlin to help Yeltsin win a second term, the paratroop general has clashed with powerful rivals such as presidential chief of staff Anatoly Chubais, who he said was behind Kulikov's bombshell allegations against him.

Parliament called on the leadership to take firm control of the country and, building on its allegation that Lebed was in league with Chechnya's rebels, asked for an investigation into anyone who might foment unrest and threaten Russia's territorial integrity.

The liberal governor of Nizhny Novgorod, Boris Nemtsov, was one of many observers who pointed to a parallel with Yeltsin's humiliation in 1987 at the hands of the last Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, whom he replaced four years later.
Rebel spokesman Movladi Udugov said the consequences of Lebed's firing were unpredictable.

"Yeltsin is helping Lebed to become Russian president," Udugov told reporters in Grozny. "He is taking him step by step to repeat his own past...I think Yeltsin, who feels a hostage to his entourage, is doing this deliberately."
